doc.title: Mike Davis interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, April 1, 2024

title: Advice for young musicians: versatility, people skills, Cole's Patreon
summary: Davis advises adding arranging, composition and Pro Tools skills, being easy to work with, and creating new income lanes, citing Cole's Patreon.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Advice to young musicians starting out

blocks.x: Let’s talk about advice you might give to young musicians today. I believe this is a quote from you from a previous interview and you said, “The inclusion of musicians on everything from CDs to film soundtracks to television commercials and Broadway shows no longer feels like a given but more like a luxury.”

Wow. If I said that I agree with myself then. Yeah, it certainly is, and I think especially now with the whole development of AI and everything that’s coming, boy there’s — the advice I would have with that in mind is become as versatile as you can become so you can deal with a lot of things and for instance by that I mean of course whatever your primary thing is, in my case it’s playing the trombone, be as good as you can possibly be in your primary thing but then also add some other tools to your toolbox. Add arranging. Add composition. If you are technically proficient be good at operating Pro Tools. If you can use Finale and understand how to copy things that’s actually also valuable. And then on top of all that, just work on your people skills you know people that work are people that other people like to be around. And you know I think, Monk, it’s probably the same as a college professor is the same as — you know people like to be around the people that they like. And so if you can make it easy for them to like you, you know don’t create a lot of problems. Don’t impose your thoughts all the time. Find out when it’s appropriate to add a comment here or there. Know what it is to go into a section and be playing third trombone and the lead trombone player has been there for 25 years and has a way of operating the section and just try to fit into that. If you have the ability to do that you’re

going to work a lot more for sure. And all those things I mean I think — I always say when I give clinics it’s like you’re opening a flower shop and there’s already five or six flower shops within a couple mile radius of you. So that’s not to say that you can’t be successful, but what’s going to make you more successful? So you know, oh that person always opens at 8:15 but it says 8:00 and, you know I hate going there because their person is always late and I need to get in and out of there so I can go to work or whatever analogy you want to use, all of those things factor in to somebody getting a call and I think now especially. The music business has always been a difficult business and it was challenging when I first started freelancing in New York, but it’s harder now and there’s less recording work, there’s less of the higher end kind of work. There’s still some, but it’s less and the level of players I would say is generally going up. So basically I’m saying the competition is even greater. Other things I would just add, just from a personal standpoint with my son Cole, who I had mentioned earlier who wrote “Open City,” he’s really developed his own Patreon channel like focusing on teaching and he does a Transcription Tuesday and he does a Monday Morning Warm-up session. He’s a bass player. And he’s gotten hundreds and hundreds of subscribers in about a year’s time and he’s really turned it into — it’s financially successful. So he figured out a way to use that tool — Patreon — and turn it into something that works for him and it enables him to use his skills in a way that can be profitable. So anything you could do like that — I’m sure there’s stuff that I’m not even aware of or have the ability to do that younger folks would take to quite naturally.
